hints: Look at the shape and position of each label in Fig. 10.1 - which are small oval bodies in the cytoplasm, which is the large fluid-filled space in the middle, and which is the outer boundary?
Remember guard cells are unusual plant cells because they contain green photosynthetic organelles and have a very large central compartment that fills with water to make them turgid.
For C, think about the tough outer layer outside the cell surface membrane that gives the guard cell its characteristic uneven thickening to allow opening and closing.
walkthrough:
Spot the Small Ovals - A**
You can see many small lens-shaped structures scattered in the cytoplasm. These are green and photosynthetic, which is special because most epidermal cells have no chloroplasts but guard cells do. So A is chloroplast.

Large Central Space and Outer Boundary - B and C**
The large fluid-filled sac in the centre that changes volume during opening and closing is the vacuole, so B is vacuole. The outermost line surrounding the whole cell is the rigid cellulose boundary, so C is cell wall.
Final answer: A - chloroplast; B - vacuole; C - cell wall.

hints: Start with where a hormone must first act - how does any chemical signal get detected by the guard cell?
Think about ions as messengers inside the cell - which positive ion enters the cytoplasm and acts as a second messenger to switch channels on and off?
Link ion movement to water potential - if solute ions leave the guard cell, what happens to its water potential and which way will water move by osmosis?
Finish the causal chain - what happens to the volume and firmness of the guard cells when they lose water, and how does that close the pore?
walkthrough:
Detection of the Stress Signal**
In water stress, abscisic acid binds to receptors on the cell surface membrane of the guard cell. This is cell signalling - the hormone is the first messenger outside. It also inhibits proton pumps, helping to depolarise the membrane.

Calcium as the Internal Switch**
Binding stimulates opening of $Ca^{2+}$ channels so $Ca^{2+}$ enters the cytoplasm. $Ca^{2+}$ acts as a second messenger inside, triggering the next changes. Think of it as relaying the message from membrane to ion channels.

Potassium Leaves - Water Potential Rises**
The calcium signal causes $K^{+}$ channels to open and $K^{+}$ diffuses out of the guard cell. Losing solute makes the cell contents less concentrated, so the water potential of the guard cell increases (becomes less negative).

Osmosis Out and Loss of Turgor**
Water now leaves the guard cell by osmosis down its water potential gradient to the surrounding cells. The guard cell volume decreases and it becomes flaccid. The thin outer walls relax and the thick inner walls come together, so the stomatal pore closes and transpiration is reduced.

Final answer: Abscisic acid binds to receptors on guard cell surface membrane; stimulates $Ca^{2+}$ uptake / opens $Ca^{2+}$ channels where $Ca^{2+}$ acts as second messenger; $K^{+}$ diffuses out of guard cell so water potential increases; water leaves by osmosis down water potential gradient, guard cells become flaccid and stoma closes.
